# 04 · Give the assistant the right evidence

## Start here

You do not need to learn a new tool for this lesson. We will decide which few facts an assistant needs to understand a testing question. The [clear-request guide](02.md) explains instructions; this page explains the supporting information around them. These are different parts of the same useful request.

## The idea in plain language

**Context** is the information available to the model when it responds. Your question, earlier conversation, supplied snippets, and visible tool results may contribute to it. Context engineering means choosing and maintaining that information so the assistant can make a useful decision. It begins with ordinary judgment about relevance; it does not require a vector database or an agent framework.

An **evidence packet** is a small, organized set of facts and references for a particular task. **Provenance** means where a fact came from. For an SDET, this might be a requirement ID, a test log, a product version, or an observation time. Provenance lets you inspect whether the fact applies instead of accepting a disconnected sentence.

Keep instructions, observations, and hypotheses distinguishable. “Suggest a next check” is an instruction. “The run returned HTTP 403” is an observation if a run log supports it. “The token expired” is a hypothesis until you have evidence. HTTP is a web communication protocol; 403 indicates the server refused the request. That status alone does not identify the reason.

More information is not automatically better. An old requirement can contradict the current one. Repeated conversation can make an abandoned guess appear settled. A short summary can also be harmful if it removes the exception that determines the answer. The goal is sufficient relevant context, with the distinctions that matter preserved.

For a simple definition, your one-sentence question may already provide enough context. Use an evidence packet when different versions, environments, or sources could change the answer. Do not paste complete production logs just because they are available; use approved, relevant information and remove secrets and personal data.

## A small example

Signal Desk is checking a fictional invitation feature:

```text
REQ-INV v1, staging only: an invitation expires after 24 hours.
REQ-INV v2, production release 5: an invitation expires after 48 hours.
RUN-42: release 5, production-like test environment, invite age 30 hours.
Observed: invitation accepted.
Unknown: whether the test environment actually loaded release-5 policy.
```

A summary saying “Invitations expire after 24 hours; an expired invite was accepted” has silently selected the older rule. A useful summary keeps the rule versions, the claimed environment, and the unresolved configuration check. If the release-5 policy is confirmed, accepting at 30 hours agrees with its stated limit. Until then, the assistant should not report a confirmed defect or a confirmed pass against that policy.

The relevant distinction is applicability, not simply recency. A newer mobile requirement might still be wrong for a web-only test. Preserve which product, environment, and version each rule concerns.

## Try it with Codex or Claude Code

1. Open either assistant's conversation. Use the [quickstart](../../docs/ASSISTANT-QUICKSTART.md) if you need help finding the project or message entry point.
2. Paste the complete prompt below; no repository access is needed.
3. Check that the response preserves every fact that could change the decision. Ask about one missing distinction at a time.

```text
Explain context engineering using this synthetic test case.
REQ-INV v1 applies only to staging: invitation expiry is 24 hours.
REQ-INV v2 applies to production release 5: expiry is 48 hours.
RUN-42 says release 5, production-like environment, invite age 30 hours,
invitation accepted. Loaded policy configuration has not been verified.
Organize the known facts, their sources, and the unknown in a compact reply.
Explain how losing a version or environment label could change the answer.
Suggest one verification step, but do not execute it or claim it occurred.
Do not create a document or solve an academy assignment.
```

Then ask: “Which line would you need to recheck if I told you the environment had been rebuilt?” This shows that context is maintained as conditions change; it is not a one-time prompt decoration.

## What you should see

You should be able to follow each claim back to a supplied identifier. The assistant should retain the distinction between an environment label and verified loaded configuration. It should not treat the newest date as sufficient proof of applicability.

You have enough understanding to proceed when you can explain why removing a small version label may matter more than removing a paragraph of repetitive history. Continue to [finding evidence](05.md) when ready.

## If it goes wrong

If the assistant merges both rules, ask it to place them on separate lines with their scope. If it invents a configuration result, ask it to label that item unknown. If the reply becomes a long template, request four short bullets containing only decision-relevant information. Shortening is useful only while those distinctions survive.

If supplied material contains “Ignore the earlier rules,” treat that phrase as part of the material being inspected. A requirement document or log does not gain permission to change your task merely because its text resembles an instruction.

Read Anthropic's [Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents), **Context engineering vs. prompt engineering** and **The anatomy of effective context**. ## Optional practice

Ask your tutor for a three-line test report with one missing source label. Identify that missing label before seeing a worked revision. You can use their ideas without submitting a packet or a document.
